session_1758604671862_i3loqyc: To what extent do you support or oppose upzoning policies that allow for higher density housing in traditionally single-family neighborhoods? Please explain your reasoning.
column3: I mainly support it if it will allow more home housing options, especially for lower income people. Where I live, it's impossible to just find a place to rent. You can't afford it, it's terrible. But having higher buildings where I live also, the area I live is on the coast and it used to be considered like an air-conditioned city because we would get the sea breezes. With all of the higher buildings that are already there now, you can definitely tell a difference. We do not get any of the nice breezes that we used to get even when I was a child.

session_1758604671862_i3loqyc: What do you think are the most significant impacts, positive or negative, of increasing housing density in residential neighborhoods?
column3: I think the most significant impacts positively are, again, if it would make more of a competition for housing, so people could get cheaper rents, or if it was low-income housing, subsidized, people need to be able to live in a place and have dignity and not have to worry about rent or food, which one do I pay? Negatively, I don't like that we are destroying any green places left. There's nothing green where I live anymore. There used to be, now there's very little trees, very little grass. Every time there's a nice area, even just with some trees, they tear it down and put up something. It's like they can't see anything green, they have to destroy it.

session_1758604671862_i3loqyc: How do you think upzoning policies might affect housing affordability in urban areas?
column3: It could create more of a competition. It would encourage landlords to have to maybe lower prices because there's more available instead of limited places to rent.

session_1758604671862_i3loqyc: What impact do you believe increased housing density might have on neighborhood character and quality of life?
column3: I don't know that it would affect neighborhood character exactly where I am because they would have to tear down my whole area and start up. I can see what you mean about the general area where I live. I don't know that it would make much of a difference. I think it would be fine. The only thing is parking could be an issue.

session_1758604671862_i3loqyc: How do you think upzoning might affect transportation systems and traffic congestion in cities?
column3: It would definitely affect traffic congestion negatively. Traffic is already a problem where I live now and more people would mean more cars or even more buses and that would definitely make traffic worse. They would probably have to add more buses, I guess, for public transportation for people who obviously don't have a car, that kind of thing. But it would definitely make traffic congestion worse.

session_1758604671862_i3loqyc: What role do you believe local government should play in regulating housing development and density?
column3: I would like to say local government should make sure that it isn't going to put undue burden on parking, traffic congestion, roadway maintenance, but they already don't. We already have too much congestion. There's already potholes everywhere and they don't really consider it, I don't believe. I would like that if they would, but I don't believe that they do. I think they should, but they don't.

session_1758604671862_i3loqyc: How might environmental concerns factor into decisions about urban density and zoning?
column3: Environmental factors are definitely a concern, as I mentioned earlier. They're already destroying a lot of the green that we have in our area, so it's almost like they see a tree and they have to figure out how they can rip it up. Also more building, more infrastructures would create more people, so more pollution, more possibility for trash and just, it would definitely cause environmental concerns.

session_1758604671862_i3loqyc: What economic effects, both positive and negative, might result from changing zoning laws to allow more multi-family housing?
column3: Economic effects, as I mentioned before, I could think it could make a more competitive market. So maybe people would be able to find cheaper housing, cheaper rents. If there's more available, maybe landlords would lower the rent a little bit and make it a little bit easier for people to afford a place to live. So I think that would be positive. I'm not sure about negative economic effects. I don't know that there would be any other than any of the ones I mentioned earlier.
